unit.title: Debt and credit
unit.description: What debt really costs, which kinds to avoid and why expensive debt comes before investing

u3l1.title: Nominal rate, APR and the real cost of a loan

texts: «Only €149 a month»
Salesman
You can drive this car away today for **only €149 a month**. Shall we sign?
What do you ask before signing?
Where do I sign? €149 works for me
The monthly payment on its own tells you nothing. For how many months? At what interest rate? How much do you pay in total?
How many months, what interest rate and how much do I pay in total?
Perfect! With those figures you can compare it with other offers.
Can you do it for €129?
Haggling over the payment without looking at the term is a trap: they can bring it down by adding years.
Erm… it's 96 months at a 9.9 % nominal rate.
8 years of payments: over **€14,300** for a car worth about €10,000. Still sure it's «only» €149?
What a loan really costs
You borrow **€6,000**. The bank offers you a 7 % nominal rate and a 3 % arrangement fee. The **APR** adds in the fees and tells you the real cost over a year.
Over 4 years, how much will you end up paying back in total, including the fee?
The €6,000 and not much more
About €1,000 more than you borrowed
Double what you borrowed
A €143.68 payment × 48 months + a €180 fee = **€7,077**. The €6,000 costs you €1,077.
With €6,000, find the term at which the loan costs you less than €500.
A low monthly payment isn't a cheap loan: it's usually a **longer** one. To compare, always look at the **APR** and how much you pay in total.
Teeny monthly payment… but look how much you pay back in total!
See how the APR is higher than the nominal rate? That's the fee.
Move the term and watch the payment and the total

steps.title: Nominal rate and APR
steps.body:
• **Nominal rate (TIN in Spain):** the «pure» interest you're charged on the money you borrow.
• **APR (TAE in Spain):** adds the compulsory **fees** and takes into account how often you pay. It's the real cost over a year.

Over 3 years, a loan at a 6 % nominal rate with a 3 % fee costs more than one at a 7.5 % nominal rate with no fee: **an APR of 8.36 % versus 7.76 %**.

And if you're thinking of investing: a loan at 7 % APR costs you that 7 % **for sure** every year.
steps.key: To compare loans, look at the APR, not the nominal rate or the monthly payment.
steps.tip: Try it: ask your tutor Lumi what your loan would cost over a different term.

texts: Japan on instalments
Marta
I'm off to Japan! The trip costs €3,000 and they'll finance it over 24 months at 18 % APR. I deserve it!
What do you tell her?
Great, go for it!
At that rate she'll pay **over €500** in interest, and she'll still be paying for the trip more than a year after she gets back.
What if you save up for a few months and go next year?
Good idea! With €250 a month she'll have it in a year, **with no interest**, and she'll enjoy the trip just as much.
Put it on the revolving card, it's easier
Even worse: the revolving card's small payment can drag the debt out for years.
Fine… but next year I'm going, no matter what!
Does it create value or destroy it?

Not all debt is the same. The kind that **can make sense** pays for something that lasts or earns you income, at a reasonable interest rate. The kind that's **best avoided** pays for something that's over before the debt is, and it's expensive too.
Can make sense
Best avoided
Mortgage with an affordable payment and your cushion in place
A flat lasts for decades and the interest is usually low… as long as you can keep up the payments.
Latest phone on a revolving credit card
It's out of date before it's paid off, and a revolving card can go over 20 % APR.
Cheap loan for training that raises your salary
If it really does boost your income, the debt pays for itself.
Holiday in 24 instalments
The trip lasts a week; the debt, two years.
Basic car you need for work, at 6 % APR
If you can't work without a car, it can make sense… as long as you don't go overboard on the car.
Payday loan to get to the end of the month
Their APRs can top 2,000 %: it plugs one hole by digging a bigger one.
Sort the six debts.

**Three questions before you sign:** will it last longer than the debt? What's the APR (above 7-8 %, it's expensive)? Could I keep paying if my income fell? Repayments on all your debts shouldn't go over **30-35 %** of your income.
Ask yourself: will this last longer than it takes me to pay it off?
Sort each debt

steps.title: Expensive debt comes before investing
steps.body:
A debt at 20 % charges you that 20 % **for sure** every year. No investment guarantees you'll earn that: not even the stock market, which has good years and very bad ones.

That's why expensive debt goes before investing. Cheap, affordable debt, like a mortgage with a reasonable payment, can live alongside your portfolio.
steps.key: If a debt costs you more than you expect to earn by investing, clear it first.
steps.tip: Try it: ask your tutor Lumi whether your debt is expensive or cheap.

u3l3.title: Revolving credit cards and payday loans

texts: The small-payment trap

You buy a laptop on your card and pick the «easy payment» option of a **revolving** card: you owe **€3,000** at 22 % and pay **€60 a month**. Sounds like little… but the payment barely covers the interest.
You owe €3,000 at 22 % and pay €60 a month. How long does it take you to pay it all off?
About 4 years
Over 11 years
You never finish
**137 months**: over 11 years, and you pay about **€5,200 in interest**, almost double what you owed.
Find the payment that clears it in 2 years or less.

The small payment is the bait: look at **how much you owe and how much you pay in total**. Raise the payment as much as you can and, once it's cleared, switch the card to paying in full at the end of the month.
At that payment you're not even covering the interest! The debt never goes down.
Years and years of payments… and the interest eats up almost the whole payment.
That's more like it! The higher the payment, the less interest you give away.
Raise the payment and see how much you save
€300 in 10 minutes
SMS
Hi! We'll lend you **€300 in 10 minutes**, no paperwork. You only pay back €390 in 30 days. Apply now
You're short on rent money. What do you do?
I'll take it, it's only €90 more
€90 on €300 for one month is an **APR of over 2,300 %**. And if you don't pay it back on time, the penalties make it grow.
I talk to my landlord or my family and go through my spending
Good: negotiating a delay or asking for help is far, far cheaper than a payday loan.
I take it and pay it back with the revolving card
Covering one expensive debt with another is the fastest way into a spiral.
Golden rule: if someone offers you **quick, easy** money, it's usually **expensive**.
If an interest rate seems abusive, complain to the bank and then to the Bank of Spain.
Try it: in Market, see how the S&P 500 goes up and down; your revolving card always charges.
Four debts, one plan

Pablo has four debts. Each month he pays the **minimum on all of them** and whatever's left over goes to just one:

• **Snowball:** the **smallest** one first.
• **Avalanche:** the one with the **highest interest** first.
Revolving card
Phone on instalments
Car loan
Master's loan
Which method will leave Pablo paying the least interest overall?
Snowball
Avalanche
Doesn't matter: they cost the same
The **avalanche** tackles the most expensive debt first, the one that racks up the most interest each month.
Try both methods and stick with the one that pays the least interest.
On the numbers alone, the **avalanche** wins. But the snowball gives you quick wins (one debt gone in a few months!), and a plan you stick to beats a perfect one you give up on.
With the snowball, Pablo clears one debt in a few months. That's motivating! Now try the avalanche.
With more extra, look how many months you knock off!
Compare the interest of the two methods

steps.title: What doesn't work (and what comes next)
steps.body:
Spreading what's left over without a plan, or taking on another expensive debt to pay off the old ones.

And a trick: when you clear a debt, **its payment gets added to the next one**. That's why the plan speeds up over time, like a growing snowball. When the last one goes, that freed-up payment becomes your **monthly contribution to invest**.
steps.key: Minimums on all of them; the rest on just one. That's how you get out of debt.
steps.tip: Try it: when you pay off a debt, buy an ETF in the simulator with that payment.

texts: Bruno's bonus
Bruno
I've just got a **€3,000** bonus. I've got a car loan at 9 % and I wanted to start investing. What do I do first?
What do you tell him?
Invest: the stock market pays more in the long run
Maybe… or maybe not: the stock market guarantees nothing. Paying off the loan is **a guaranteed 9 %**.
Pay off the loan: it's a guaranteed 9 %
That's it! Paying off a debt early gives you a **guaranteed return equal to its interest rate**. At 9 %, paying it off almost always wins.
Leave it in your account and see what happens
Sitting in the account at almost 0 % while you pay 9 % interest: you lose on both sides.
What if it were my mortgage at 2 %?
Then it's a different story. Let's sort it out
Cushion, pay off or invest?
**The rule:** paying off a debt is the same as earning its interest rate risk-free. But first things first: your cushion for the unexpected.
Cushion first
Pay it off
Investing can make sense
Revolving card at 21 %, cushion in place
Paying it off is a guaranteed 21 %: no investment guarantees that.
A debt at 8 % and no savings for emergencies
If you empty your account and something breaks down, you'll end up borrowing again, and at a higher rate.
Fixed-rate mortgage at 2 %, 6-month cushion and 20 years to go
With debt that cheap and your cushion in place, you can pay it off and invest for the long term at the same time.
Car loan at 9 %, cushion in place
Above 7-8 %, paying it off almost always wins.
Loan from your family at 0 %, cushion in place
Paying off at 0 % earns you nothing (though owing your family weighs on you too).
Decide what Bruno would do in each case.

**In order:** emergency fund, expensive debts (over 7-8 %) and then long-term investing; pay off cheap ones early if it gives you peace of mind, checking first whether there's a fee. Try it: tell your tutor Lumi your situation and ask where to start.
Ask yourself first: does he have a cushion? Then look at the debt's interest rate.
What would Bruno do in each case?

u3l1-1.prompt: To compare loans you need to look at the ____, because it includes the fees.
options: nominal rate
IBAN
monthly payment
APR
u3l1-1.explanation: The APR covers the interest, the compulsory fees and how often you pay: it's the comparable cost.

u3l1-2.prompt: Loan A: 6 % nominal rate and a 3 % arrangement fee. Loan B: 7.5 % nominal rate with no fees. Same amount and term (3 years). Which is cheaper?
options: They cost the same
B, because its APR is lower
A, because its nominal rate is lower
u3l1-2.explanation: APR of A ≈ 8.36 %; of B ≈ 7.76 %. The arrangement fee makes A dearer even though its nominal rate is lower.

u3l1-7.prompt: Match each term with what it means.
options: Nominal rate
APR
Arrangement fee
Longer term
u3l1-7.explanation: To compare loans: same amount, same term and the lowest APR.
right: The yearly cost with fees included
A payment on signing that pushes up the APR
Lower payment and more interest in total

u3l1-10.prompt: What can make a loan more expensive? Tick all.
options: A longer term
Paying it back early with no penalty
Compulsory linked insurance
A lower nominal rate with the same fees
u3l1-10.explanation: A longer term and compulsory insurance make the loan dearer, as does an arrangement fee. Paying it back early with no penalty or a lower nominal rate make it cheaper.

u3l1-11.prompt: You want to start investing and the bank offers you a personal loan at 9 % APR to do it «in a big way». What do you do?
options: I don't take it: I start with what I save
I take it: the stock market goes up more than 9 % in the long run
I borrow half, just in case
u3l1-11.explanation: The debt charges a guaranteed 9 %; the investment, on the other hand, can fall just when the payment is due. It's tempting to think the market always goes up, but in the short run nobody guarantees it.
feedback: With no interest to pay, any gain is yours, and a fall doesn't leave you owing money.
You'd have to earn over 9 % every year just to break even, and the payment arrives even if the market falls.
Less risk than borrowing it all, but you still owe a guaranteed 9 % for something that isn't guaranteed.

u3l1-12.prompt: Lumi is offered a car at 0 % TIN and thinks financing it is free. What do you reply?
options: Ask them to stretch the term so you pay less
Sign: at 0 % you pay nothing
First ask for the APR and the total cost
u3l1-12.explanation: A 0 % nominal rate can hide opening fees or tied insurance that only show up in the APR and the total to pay. It's tempting to stick with the «0 %», but what you compare is the APR.
feedback: A lower payment, but more months paying interest and fees.
The nominal rate doesn't include fees or compulsory insurance: look at the APR.
That's it! With fees and insurance, a 0 % nominal rate can turn out expensive.
lines: The dealer is offering me the car at a 0 % nominal rate.
It's free! Shall I sign now?

u3l2-2.prompt: Match each debt with its description.
options: 25-year mortgage
Revolving credit card
Loan for training
Payday loan
u3l2-2.explanation: The interest rate and what the money is used for decide whether a debt helps or sinks you.
right: Expensive debt that drags on endlessly
Quick money at a sky-high cost
A home that lasts longer than the debt

u3l2-4.prompt: A debt at 20 % APR is expensive debt.
options: True
False
u3l2-4.explanation: Well above 7-8 %: you need to get rid of it as soon as possible.

options: A revolving card to pay for a trip this summer
A mortgage with a payment of 25 % of your income
A payday loan for a concert
u3l2-7.explanation: Cheap, for something that lasts and with an affordable payment.

u3l2-8.prompt: Lumi wants a €1,200 phone and the shop will finance it over 24 months, «only €60 a month». What do you tell her?
options: Better get a €2,000 one, the payment barely goes up
Look at the APR and how much you'll pay in total
Great, that way you won't notice it!
u3l2-8.explanation: Before financing a treat, multiply the payment by the number of months.
feedback: That only stretches the debt for something that loses value very quickly.
Nice! 60 × 24 = €1,440: €240 in interest. Saving up for a few months might work out better.
You will notice: 60 × 24 = €1,440. You pay €240 more for something that will be worth much less in 2 years.
lines: I want to buy the new €1,200 phone
The shop will finance it over 24 months, only €60 a month!

u3l2-9.prompt: Pablo can borrow €6,000 at 6 % APR for a certified course after which, in his sector, salaries usually rise by about €300 a month. He has a cushion. What does he do?
options: Puts it on the revolving card so as not to take out a loan
Borrows €10,000 to treat himself to something too
Checks the payment fits and takes the loan
u3l2-9.explanation: The same debt can be good or bad: it depends on the cost and what it gives you back.
feedback: Same purchase, but at a much higher interest rate.
He mixes a debt that creates value with one that destroys it.
If the pay rise comes, the debt pays for itself in a short time: it's debt that can create value.

u3l2-10.prompt: Before you start investing, do you clear this debt or can it live alongside your portfolio?
options: Fixed mortgage at 2 % with an affordable payment
Instalment purchase at 18 %
Payday loan
Revolving card at 22 %
Student loan at 3 %
u3l2-10.explanation: Expensive debt charges more, for sure, than any investment can promise you, so it goes first. With cheap, affordable debt there's less of a rush: paying it off early only saves you its interest, and you can invest at the same time.

u3l3-3.prompt: Tick the messages that are a debt trap or a scam.
options: You've switched your card to paying in full at the end of the month. No more interest will be charged for deferring.
Congratulations! Pay for all your purchases in easy instalments of just €25 a month. Activate it now.
We'll cancel all your debts. You just have to pay €200 in admin fees upfront by Bizum.
€300 in 10 minutes, no paperwork, no questions asked! Pay back just €390 in 30 days.
Reminder: your loan has 14 payments left. APR: 7.2 %.
u3l3-3.explanation: Instant money with no questions, minimum payments that hide the debt and upfront payments to «cancel debts» are warning signs.

u3l3-4.prompt: Why is a revolving card so expensive?
options: Because it charges a fee on every purchase in shops
Because it can only be used outside Spain
Because the payment barely reduces the debt
u3l3-4.explanation: With a €30 payment on €1,000 at 2 % a month, only €10 reduces the debt in the first month.

u3l3-5.prompt: Switching your card to paying in full at the end of the month avoids paying interest for deferring.
options: True
False
u3l3-5.explanation: You pay what you've spent in one go, with no deferral and no interest.

u3l3-6.prompt: Ana owes €2,000 on a revolving card at 22 % APR and pays €50 a month. She has €4,000 in an account at 2 %, and her ideal cushion is €2,000. What does she do?
options: Invests the €4,000 in the stock market to earn more than 22 %
Uses €2,000 to clear the revolving card and keeps €2,000 as a cushion
Leaves everything as it is
u3l3-6.explanation: Paying off expensive debt is the best guaranteed «investment» there is.
feedback: No investment guarantees 22 %; the debt, on the other hand, definitely charges it.
She saves a guaranteed 22 % and still has a cushion: she wins on every front.
She earns 2 % in the account while paying 22 % on the card: she loses about €400 a year.

u3l3-7.prompt: What helps you get out of a revolving card? Tick all.
options: Paying it off with a payday loan
Paying only the minimum each month
Raising the monthly payment
Stopping using it
u3l3-7.explanation: Stopping using it and raising the payment (or switching to paying at the end of the month) cuts the debt. Paying only the minimum drags it out for years, and covering it with a payday loan makes it dearer.

u3l3-9.prompt: A €300 payday loan where you pay back €390 after 30 days has an APR of over ____.
u3l3-9.explanation: 30 % in one month, compounded over a year, is over 2,300 %.

u3l4-1.prompt: Avalanche method: put in order which debt you tackle first.
options: Car loan: €6,000 at 7 %
Loan from a relative: €500 at 0 %
Instalment purchase: €800 at 12 %
Revolving card: €1,200 at 22 %
u3l4-1.explanation: In the avalanche, the interest rate rules: highest to lowest.

u3l4-2.prompt: Snowball method with the same debts: put them in order from first to last.
options: Instalment purchase: €800 at 12 %
Revolving card: €1,200 at 22 %
Car loan: €6,000 at 7 %
Loan from a relative: €500 at 0 %
u3l4-2.explanation: In the snowball, the balance rules: smallest to largest.

u3l4-3.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
options: Avalanche
Snowball
Minimum payment
Snowball effect
u3l4-3.explanation: In both methods you pay the minimum on all of them and put the extra into one.
right: What you pay on all the others
The freed-up payment is added to the next one

u3l4-6.prompt: Pablo has tried the avalanche twice and given up: his big debt never seems to end and he loses heart. What does he do?
options: Takes out a payday loan to pay it all off in one go
Stops paying the big one for a while
Tries the snowball to get some motivation
u3l4-6.explanation: The best method is the one you manage to stick to.
feedback: He swaps several debts for one extremely expensive one: the problem grows.
Surcharges, late-payment interest and possibly ending up on a bad-debtor register.
He clears two small debts in a few months and gets his drive back. He pays a little more interest, but he doesn't give up.

u3l4-7.prompt: Laura gets a €1,000 bonus. She owes €1,000 on a revolving card at 21 % and €4,000 on her car at 6 %. What does she do with the bonus?
options: Clears the revolving card
Splits it half and half between the two
Pays €1,000 off the car early
u3l4-7.explanation: With extra money, the first debt to go is the one with the highest interest.
feedback: She gets rid of the most expensive debt and frees up that payment for the car.
She keeps the 21 % debt alive: she pays expensive interest she could have avoided.
She saves 6 % when she could have saved 21 %.

u3l4-10.prompt: What's a bad idea if you have several debts? Tick all.
options: Stopping paying the minimum on one of them
Paying the minimum on all and the extra on one
Starting with the debt with the highest interest
Taking out a payday loan to pay off the card
u3l4-10.explanation: Missing a minimum payment or covering the card with a payday loan makes things worse. Paying the minimum on all and putting the extra into one, starting with the dearest, is exactly the method.

u3l4-11.prompt: Pablo has just paid off his last expensive debt and now has €300 a month free that used to go on payments. He already has an emergency fund. What does he do?
options: He leaves it in his current account
He raises his spending: he's earned it after all that effort
He turns it into automatic saving and investing
u3l4-11.explanation: Pablo was already living without that €300, so investing it costs him nothing day to day. Raising his spending is tempting as a reward, but it stops dead the momentum he'd built.
feedback: With nowhere to go, it gets spent and loses purchasing power too.
Tempting, but he misses the best chance to start investing without noticing.
He lives just as before, but now that €300 works for him.

u3l5-3.prompt: Bruno has a fixed-rate mortgage at 2 %, a 6-month cushion and another €10,000 saved that he won't need for 15 years. What does he do?
options: Takes out another loan to invest more
Compares the guaranteed 2 % from paying off with long-term, diversified investing, without touching his cushion
Puts it all into a single trendy share because the mortgage is cheap
u3l5-3.explanation: With cheap debt there's no single right answer: what matters is comparing properly and not touching the cushion.
feedback: Borrowing to invest multiplies the risk.
He understands what he gains with each option and can split between the two.
A single company can collapse: that's not comparing, it's gambling.

u3l5-4.prompt: Marta has €3,000 on a revolving card at 21 % and another €3,000 she wants to start investing in a fund. What does she do first?
options: Pays off the revolving card
Invests the €3,000 and keeps paying the card
Invests half and pays off half
u3l5-4.explanation: Investing with a 21 % debt is filling a leaky bucket.
feedback: She locks in a risk-free 21 % a year. Then she invests what she used to pay each month.
To come out ahead, the fund would have to return more than 21 % a year.
Better than nothing, but it keeps a 21 % debt alive.

u3l5-7.prompt: You have a debt at 4 %. What does paying it off give you?
options: 4 % that could turn negative
A guaranteed 4 %
Nothing, because you don't earn interest
u3l5-7.explanation: What you no longer pay is a guaranteed gain equal to the interest rate.

u3l5-9.prompt: Lumi has a mortgage at 2 % and €200 to spare each month: she can't decide whether to pay it down or invest. What do you tell her?
options: It depends: compare the guaranteed 2 % with investing for the long term, and check you have a cushion
Invest in whatever has gone up most this year
Always pay it off: any debt is bad and you should get rid of it
u3l5-9.explanation: Paying off gives a guaranteed return; investing, an expected one. With cheap debt, both options can make sense.
feedback: That's it: with cheap debt there's no single answer; what matters is understanding what you're comparing.
That's not comparing: it's chasing trends.
Not always: at 2 % it's cheap debt. It depends on your cushion, your time horizon and your peace of mind.
lines: I've got a mortgage at 2 % and €200 a month left over.
Should I pay it off or invest?

u3l5-10.prompt: Put the usual priorities for your money in order.
options: Emergency fund
Investing for the long term
Getting rid of expensive debt
Knowing how much you spend
u3l5-10.explanation: The money pyramid: without a base, any surprise forces you to sell at the worst moment.
